significance.justification: A verified-true result would establish that sign-flipping the optimization objective installs an opposite latent trait and that "the magnitude of the anti-trait predicts the magnitude of ordinary positive transfer"—a form-(iii) quantitative coupling, combined with a form-(ii) causal mechanism involving an anti-aligned steering direction. This would establish both a behavioral phenomenon (opposite-trait transfer from innocuous data) and a mechanism, while constraining predictions across traits and strengths rather than merely identifying another transferable direction; this directly bears on the gradient-alignment account underlying Cloud et al.'s Subliminal Learning work, which reports hidden trait transmission through semantically unrelated data. A negative result—especially failure of anti-alignment despite ordinary transfer—would rule out sign-linear gradient alignment as a sufficient explanation, although it would not resolve subliminal learning's broader mechanism; verified-true and verified-false are therefore distinct and informative states. Topic substitution fails: merely proposing another extension of subliminal learning would not merit this score, whereas the specific sign-symmetry law and its mechanistic consequence place this above the topic-median hypothesis.

reach.justification: The named handle is "Inverse Subliminal Learning": a "sign-flipped objective" intended as a "label-free inoculation," together with transfer-strength symmetry as a predictor of the attainable anti-trait. It is ex ante because it would modify a student before deployment using an undesirable teacher's innocuous data, leaving an action window for trainers or deployment practitioners rather than merely explaining a failure afterward. After per-model re-extraction, the symmetry conclusion would still predict the sign and approximate magnitude of the result, so more than a search procedure transfers; however, the asserted dependence on matched bases and a likely local linear regime limits it short of a broadly invariant design law. The hypothesis asserts applicability across traits and model families and could affect researchers who train, audit, or gate models; topic substitution fails because the generic subliminal-learning topic supplies neither this intervention nor its forward-looking sign/magnitude prediction.
